deferredTracks.legalDesignRationale: The review's decision is "Additional research required", with the express instruction to screen for it, name it accurately, and not generate a packet until the interaction between the RSA 265-A:21 ten-year clock and the RSA 651:5, III completion requirement is settled. The refresh confirmed the two rules at source but could not reconcile them: RSA 265-A:21, I fixes its bar to the date of conviction and RSA 651:5, III runs from completion of all terms and conditions, and neither section addresses the other. The waiting period is therefore an undetermined element of the design, so no output strategy is asserted and the track is preserved as a deferred entry rather than built on a guess. The refresh did add one substantive finding the review flagged and the internal reference missed: the permanent-file retention, openable only for sentencing under RSA 265-A:3, is confirmed in the statutory text and must be disclosed whenever this track is eventually built.
deferredTracks.mechanism: RSA 265-A:21, I operates notwithstanding RSA 651:5, and RSA 651:5, III opens with an express exception for it. No court shall order annulment of a conviction for driving or attempting to drive a vehicle, for operating or attempting to operate or being in actual physical control of an OHRV, or for operating or attempting to operate a boat on New Hampshire waters, while under the influence or with an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more, or for aggravated drunken driving, until ten years after the date of conviction. The section was read at gc.nh.gov on 2026-08-06 and the clock runs from the date of conviction, not from completion of the sentence, which is different from every other New Hampshire conviction track. Any record annulled under the section shall be retained in a permanent file, to be opened only for purposes of sentencing in the case of an offence under RSA 265-A:3. Relief is discretionary under RSA 651:5, I once the ten-year bar has run; RSA 265-A:21 is a prohibition on early annulment, not a grant.

deferredTracks.mechanism: Any person convicted of a criminal offence which occurred between May 14, 2014 and July 1, 2015 while the person was 17 years of age shall be entitled to an annulment of that conviction upon application to the court. The only permitted basis for denial is a written finding by the court, on clear and convincing evidence, that the offence would have qualified for transfer to the superior court under RSA 169-B:24 and that the prosecution would have pursued such transfer. Annulment requests under the section are not subject to any filing fee. These are adult criminal convictions entered against people who were 17 during the window before New Hampshire raised the age of juvenile jurisdiction, so the records sit in the adult system and the relief belongs in ordinary adult scope. The section operates notwithstanding RSA 651:5, so the paragraph V bars and the paragraph VI whole-record rule appear not to apply, which if correct makes this the strongest relief in the state. deferredTracks.legalDesignRationale: Additional research required, as counsel decided, and high value: it converts ineligible participants into eligible ones. deferredTracks.mechanism: Section 12-1.3-1(5) provides that 'misdemeanor' includes, but is not limited to, those crimes previously classified as felonies under law at the time the original sentence was imposed but reclassified by the general assembly as a misdemeanor in the interim, prior to the time the motion to expunge is brought. A participant whose old conviction was a felony when imposed but is a misdemeanor today is therefore treated as a misdemeanant for expungement purposes, which moves them from the ten-year felony wait to the five-year misdemeanor wait and may make them eligible for the multiple-misdemeanor route they would otherwise be excluded from by the no-felony-conviction condition. This is an overlay on the first-offender misdemeanor and multiple-misdemeanor routes rather than a standalone remedy, and it is separated here because it has its own authority, its own effective date and its own factual test.

deferredTracks.legalDesignRationale: Additional research required, as counsel decided. Reading § 23A-27-53 at the official source confirmed the mechanism and added two eligibility facts, but it did not answer the question that matters for record clearing: what record remains once the original charge is dismissed and the defendant stands convicted of the lesser ingestion or possession offence. The mechanism is a plea-bargaining structure rather than a record-clearing one, and its interaction with the arrest and SIS tracks is not established. deferredTracks.mechanism: After receiving a plea of guilty for a violation of § 22-42-5 or § 22-42-5.1 a court may, without entering a judgment of guilt and with the consent of the defendant, defer imposition of sentence and place the defendant on probation on terms that must include a drug and alcohol evaluation and any recommended course of treatment. If after one year the defendant has completed treatment and complied with all conditions, the court shall dismiss the § 22-42-5 or § 22-42-5.1 charge upon the defendant pleading guilty to ingestion under § 22-42-15 or possession under § 22-42-15.1. No person previously granted a deferred imposition of sentence is eligible for a second. A defendant is ineligible where aggravating circumstances exist as defined by § 22-6-11, or where the defendant is serving a sentence under the supervision of the executive branch.

The narrower statutory formulation should replace the general description.
